title: Gestational Diabetes: Postnatal Follow-Up for Type 2 Diabetes Risk

evidenceAudit.scope: Women who had gestational diabetes, after birth and in primary care: stopping treatment, postpartum glucose checks, the 6–13 week diabetes test, annual testing and planning the next pregnancy. Checked against the Saudi MOH Pocket Manual in Obstetrics & Gynaecology (2014) and NICE NG3. Sections: MOH pp. 170–171; NG3 recommendations 1.6.3, 1.6.8–1.6.15.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 14 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: The MOH manual is a 2014 document and gives no postpartum OGTT interpretation cut-offs; the diabetes thresholds here are the NICE fasting glucose and HbA1c values.
NICE and the MOH differ on the diabetes test (fasting glucose 6–13 weeks versus a 75-g OGTT at 6–12 weeks); both are shown and local protocol decides.
The NICE National Diabetes Prevention Programme is a UK service; the Saudi equivalent was not assessed.
Contraception choice follows the MOH statement that any method is acceptable without medical contraindication; the UK eligibility criteria were not opened.
SFDA registration was not assessed; no medicines are recommended in this topic.

pathophysiology.summary: Women with gestational diabetes have a markedly higher risk of developing type 2 diabetes after the pregnancy, so structured testing is needed even when glucose returns to normal at birth (summarised from NG3 1.6.9–1.6.14). Hyperglycaemia usually settles quickly after delivery, so glucose-lowering treatment is stopped immediately after birth (NG3 1.6.3). Glucose is tested before transfer to community care to exclude persisting hyperglycaemia (NG3 1.6.8). Women with gestational diabetes may have recurrence in future pregnancies and should be offered early testing then (NG3 1.6.10, 1.6.15).

symptoms: Frequent urination, excessive thirst, weight loss or fatigue suggest diabetes; the woman should see her doctor (NG3 1.6.9).
No symptoms is common; testing is by schedule, not symptoms.
physicalSigns: Weight and BMI at the postnatal review.
Blood pressure at the postnatal review.
redFlags: Symptoms of hyperglycaemia (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss, fatigue) after birth: test glucose that day (NG3 1.6.9).
Fasting glucose 7.0 mmol/L or above, or HbA1c 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or above: likely type 2 diabetes; confirm or refer (NG3 1.6.12–1.6.13).
Persisting hyperglycaemia before transfer to community care: do not discharge without a plan (NG3 1.6.8).
precipitants: Gestational diabetes in the index pregnancy (NG3 1.6.10).
Hyperglycaemia needing insulin or tablets in pregnancy.

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: Fasting glucose 7.0 mmol/L or above or HbA1c 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or above after birth (NG3 1.6.12–1.6.13).
Fasting glucose 6.0–6.9 mmol/L or HbA1c 39–47 mmol/mol (5.7–6.4%) (NG3 1.6.12–1.6.13).
Fasting glucose below 6.0 mmol/L or HbA1c below 39 mmol/mol (5.7%); still needs annual testing (NG3 1.6.12–1.6.14).

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Woman with prior gestational diabetes whose glucose normalised after birth
ruleIn.expectedFinding: 6.0–6.9 mmol/L high risk; 7.0 mmol/L or above likely type 2 diabetes, confirm with a test (NG3 1.6.12).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Offer 6 to 13 weeks after birth, which may coincide with the 6-week check; offer after 13 weeks if not already done (NG3 1.6.11).

references.title: NICE NG3: Diabetes in pregnancy: management from preconception to the postnatal period

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Woman after 13 weeks postpartum when fasting glucose is not possible, and for annual review
ruleIn.expectedFinding: 39–47 mmol/mol high risk; 48 mmol/mol or above type 2 diabetes, refer (NG3 1.6.13).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Annual HbA1c after a negative postnatal test (NG3 1.6.14).

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Woman with prior gestational diabetes under Saudi MOH practice
ruleIn.targetCondition: Type 2 diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Abnormal result establishes diabetes or impaired glucose tolerance; use local postpartum criteria (MOH p. 171).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: MOH advises all women with gestational diabetes have this at 6–12 weeks postpartum; NICE uses fasting glucose instead (MOH p. 171; NG3 1.6.11).
ruleIn.normalValue: Result interpreted by local postpartum criteria

references.title: MOH Pocket Manual in Obstetrics & Gynaecology, Saudi Ministry of Health

ruleOut.expectedFinding: Raised glucose before transfer needs diabetes review (NG3 1.6.8).
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: MOH checks fasting and after meals for 24 hours after vaginal birth and 48 hours after caesarean, keeping glucose 140–160 mg/dL (MOH p. 171).

references.title: NICE NG3: Diabetes in pregnancy: management from preconception to the postnatal period

clinicalManagement.title: After the birth
actions: Check glucose fasting and after meals for 24 hours after vaginal birth and 48 hours after caesarean; keep 140–160 mg/dL (MOH p. 171).
Test glucose before transfer to community care (NG3 1.6.8).

clinicalManagement.title: Advice before discharge
actions: Remind the woman of the symptoms of hyperglycaemia (NG3 1.6.9).
Explain the risk of recurrence and offer diabetes testing when planning future pregnancies (NG3 1.6.10).
Contraception: any method is acceptable without medical contraindication (MOH p. 171).

clinicalManagement.title: Diabetes test
actions: NICE: fasting plasma glucose at 6–13 weeks, or HbA1c after 13 weeks if fasting is not possible (NG3 1.6.11).
Act on the result: below 6.0 mmol/L annual test; 6.0–6.9 high risk and prevention advice; 7.0 or above confirm diabetes (NG3 1.6.12). HbA1c 39–47 high risk, 48 or above refer (NG3 1.6.13).

clinicalManagement.title: Annual follow-up
actions: Offer annual HbA1c after a negative postnatal test (NG3 1.6.14).
Advise to see the GP if symptoms of diabetes develop (NG3 1.6.9).
Refer into the diabetes prevention service if eligible; offer lifestyle advice for high-risk results (NG3 1.6.11–1.6.12).

clinicalManagement.title: Next pregnancy
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Before and early in a future pregnancy
actions: Offer early self-monitoring of glucose or an OGTT in the next pregnancy, with a second OGTT at 24–28 weeks if normal (NG3 1.6.15, 1.2.6).
Women with diabetes planning pregnancy should take folic acid; NICE advises 5 mg a day until 12 weeks (NG3 1.1).

medicationPlan.note: No medicine is recommended in this topic. Glucose-lowering therapy for gestational diabetes is stopped immediately after birth (NICE NG3 1.6.3). Medicines for diabetes found at follow-up follow the repository's type 2 diabetes topics.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Stop glucose-lowering therapy immediately after birth for gestational diabetes (NG3 1.6.3)
Test glucose to exclude persisting hyperglycaemia (NG3 1.6.8); MOH: glucose checks for 24 hours after vaginal birth and 48 hours after caesarean, keep 140–160 mg/dL (MOH p. 171)
NICE: fasting plasma glucose 6 to 13 weeks, or HbA1c if not possible after 13 weeks; MOH: 75-g 2-hour OGTT at 6–12 weeks (NG3 1.6.11; MOH p. 171)
Below 6.0 mmol/L normal, annual test; 6.0–6.9 mmol/L high risk; 7.0 mmol/L or above likely type 2 diabetes, confirm (NG3 1.6.12)
Below 39 mmol/mol (5.7%) normal; 39–47 mmol/mol high risk; 48 mmol/mol (6.5%) or above type 2 diabetes (NG3 1.6.13)
Annual HbA1c after a negative postnatal test (NG3 1.6.14)

guidelineComparison.title: Saudi MOH Pocket Manual (2014) versus NICE NG3 postnatal follow-up

values: Fasting and after meals for 24 hours (vaginal) or 48 hours (caesarean); keep 140–160 mg/dL (p. 171)
Test glucose before transfer to community care (1.6.8)
Fasting glucose 6–13 weeks, or HbA1c after 13 weeks (1.6.11)
Annual HbA1c after a negative test (1.6.14)

guidelineComparison.note: The MOH manual gives no cut-offs for the postpartum OGTT; use local criteria. The NICE fasting glucose and HbA1c thresholds apply to the NICE pathway.

teaching.scope: Women who had gestational diabetes, after birth and in primary care: stopping treatment, postpartum glucose checks, the 6–13 week diabetes test, annual testing and planning the next pregnancy. Checked against the Saudi MOH Pocket Manual in Obstetrics & Gynaecology (2014) and NICE NG3. Sections: MOH pp. 170–171; NG3 recommendations 1.6.3, 1.6.8–1.6.15.
learningObjectives: Stop treatment after birth and arrange the correct diabetes test at 6 to 13 weeks.
Interpret the fasting glucose and HbA1c results and set annual follow-up.
pitfalls: Continuing metformin or insulin after birth.
Not testing at all because glucose was normal at discharge.
Treating the single negative test as permanent reassurance.
Missing early testing in the next pregnancy.
keyPoints: Stop glucose-lowering therapy immediately after birth.
NICE: fasting glucose 6–13 weeks; MOH: OGTT 6–12 weeks.
Fasting 6.0–6.9 or HbA1c 39–47: high risk; 7.0 or 48 and above: diabetes.
Annual HbA1c after a negative test.

patientEducation: Explain that gestational diabetes raises the risk of type 2 diabetes later and that annual testing is needed (NG3 1.6.10, 1.6.14).
Teach the symptoms of hyperglycaemia and to see the GP if they appear (NG3 1.6.9).
Explain the need for early glucose testing in future pregnancies (NG3 1.6.15).
lifestyleAndDiet: Keep a healthy weight and be physically active, with support if eligible for a diabetes prevention programme (NG3 1.6.11–1.6.12).
Follow dietary advice from the pregnancy dietitian and extend healthy eating to the family.
mdtReferrals: Primary care for the 6–13 week test and annual HbA1c (NG3 1.6.11, 1.6.14).
Diabetes service for a confirmed diagnosis (NG3 1.6.12–1.6.13).
Dietitian or diabetes prevention programme for high-risk results (NG3 1.6.12).
dischargeCriteria: Glucose-lowering treatment stopped and glucose checked before transfer (NG3 1.6.3, 1.6.8).
Date of the 6–13 week diabetes test booked (NG3 1.6.11).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Diabetes test at 6 to 13 weeks (NICE) or 6 to 12 weeks (MOH), then annual HbA1c after a negative result, and early testing in any future pregnancy (NG3 1.6.11, 1.6.14–1.6.15; MOH p. 171).
